text: Michael Ulis, Gavin Crowley, and Thaddeus Poff

Our project focuses on motor control, specifically analyzing how individuals move their hands while reaching toward targets.
The overall goal is to eventually estimate how quickly participants begin correcting their movements in response to changes in the visual environment.
For this stage of the project, we focused on exploratory data analysis to better understand the dataset and identify important patterns before moving into modeling.

Our dataset contains 1,200 individual reaching trials from two participants. Each participant completed two experimental conditions, with three blocks of 100 trials per condition.
The data were collected at 1,000 Hertz, meaning hand movements were recorded every millisecond. This gives us very detailed time-series measurements.
The primary variables we examined were hand position, velocity, and acceleration, particularly in the lateral or side-to-side direction.
One important preprocessing step was aligning every trial to its recorded Pixel event. We defined this event as time zero and examined movement from 200 milliseconds before to 500 milliseconds after it.
This allowed us to compare and average movement trajectories across different trials.

We also examined how frequently each participant successfully reached the target.
We classified trials as hits or misses using the event information recorded in the CSV files.
Overall, approximately 81% of trials were successful. However, there was a substantial difference between participants.
Participant A had a hit rate of 67.5%, compared with 94.3% for Participant B, a difference of approximately 27 percentage points.
We also observed some variation across experimental conditions. Participant A performed better in Condition B, while Participant B performed slightly better in Condition A.
Something that was interesting was that fast and slow targets had nearly identical overall hit rates.

Finally, we wanted to visualize how hand movement changes over time.
This graph shows average lateral hand velocity for Participant A in Condition A, using slow-target trials from all three blocks.
We aligned every trial to the Pixel event, shown by the dashed vertical line at zero milliseconds, and calculated the average velocity at each time point for the three background categories.
Before the event, all three categories follow relatively similar patterns, with velocity increasing toward zero.
After the event, velocity continues increasing, but the curves begin to diverge later in the movement.
This shows that there are differences in average movement trajectories across background categories.
We also examined acceleration, which will be particularly important for estimating corrective movement onset. However, those signals were much noisier, and the average did not show a clear corrective response.
Before proceeding to modeling, we'll need to clarify how leftward and rightward corrective movements are identified so that we can properly preprocess and interpret the acceleration data.

text: Median duration: A 177 ms, B 220.5 ms. Peak searches stop at each trial’s outcome.

After viewing the velocity traces, we checked how much of that plotting window actually falls within each trial's response window. The project defines the response-search interval from the Pixel event to the Got target or Missed target event. Both hits and misses remain in this check.

This chart groups the duration of that interval into 100 ms bins. Each participant contributes 600 trials. Participant A has a median duration of 177 ms and Participant B has a median of 220.5 ms. The full dataset ranges from 31 to 449 ms, so every trial ends before +500 ms.

This matters for the earlier velocity plot. Its later samples are useful context, but many occur after the target outcome. An onset analysis that searches the entire fixed window could select a later movement instead of the response of interest. We therefore search for peaks only within each trial's own event window and mark its endpoint on example plots.

This is a descriptive timing difference, not evidence that one participant has a later corrective onset. The average at a late time can also contain a different subset of trials because shorter trials have ended.

Source: 02_exploratory_analysis.qmd, “Quality, retention, and event timing” and “All participants, conditions, speeds, and blocks.” Numeric source: eda_output/trial_quality_audit.csv, End_ms, all 1,200 trials. Bin intervals are [0,100), [100,200), [200,300), [300,400), [400,500) ms.

name: Google Shape;172;p4
text: Baseline SD is about 2.4–2.5 m/s². The prescribed thresholds are 0.20 and 0.125 m/s².

Next, we quantified the pre-event acceleration fluctuations instead of relying only on how noisy the curves look. For each trial, we calculated the standard deviation of unsmoothed position-derived acceleration from -200 to -20 ms relative to the Pixel event. The four blue bars show the median of those trial-level SD values within each participant and condition, pooling backgrounds, target speeds, and blocks. Each group has 300 trials.

The medians are Participant A, Condition A: 2.46 m/s²; Participant A, Condition B: 2.43 m/s²; Participant B, Condition A: 2.49 m/s²; Participant B, Condition B: 2.50 m/s². The two smaller bars show the magnitudes of the project thresholds: 0.20 m/s² for ordinary GMR and 0.125 m/s² for threshold alignment. These are threshold magnitudes, not additional estimates of baseline SD.

The baseline is part of an ongoing reaching movement, so its variability includes actual movement as well as measurement or differentiation noise. This comparison does not prove that the thresholds are wrong. It shows why a single excursion above threshold cannot by itself establish corrective onset, especially in an unsmoothed signal. The median trial spends about 93.9% of its baseline samples outside ±0.20 m/s². This is a descriptive amplitude check, not a false-positive onset rate.

We also checked whether differentiation or importing the data caused the discrepancy. Twice-differentiated position closely reproduces the supplied acceleration, with a maximum trial RMSE below 9 × 10^-12 m/s² in these data. Thus, the noisy signal is not explained by a simple mismatch between those acceleration sources.

Before estimating onset, we need to confirm the left/right response signs and evaluate any filtering choice. The project method works backward from the relevant positive response peak to the last upward crossing. We have not reported onset results here.

Source: 02_exploratory_analysis.qmd, “Validate position-derived acceleration” and “Baseline noise, polarity, and threshold feasibility.” Numeric sources: eda_output/trial_features.csv, Baseline_SD and Fraction_outside_020, and eda_output/signal_agreement.csv, RMSE.

text: Smoothing reduces fluctuations and can move threshold crossings. Filter choice remains open.

Finally, we explored how sensitive acceleration is to preprocessing. This is one recorded left-background, slow-target trial from Participant A, Condition A, Block 1, Trial 12. The Pixel event occurs at time zero and the recorded miss ends its response-search window 94 ms later. Negative times show pre-event context only. The vertical dotted line marks the Pixel event.

All three curves start with the same hand-position data. The gray curve differentiates raw position twice. The blue and orange curves first apply centered moving averages to position over 11 ms or 21 ms, then differentiate twice using 1 ms sampling. These are example windows from the Quarto sensitivity analysis, not recommended filters.

The example's pre-event acceleration SD changes from 2.46 m/s² without smoothing to 0.368 m/s² with the 11 ms position window and 0.256 m/s² with the 21 ms window. All curves use the same vertical scale so the audience can see the magnitude of the change. The smoother curves lie close to zero on that scale.

A smoother curve does not automatically give a more accurate onset. A centered average can spread post-event information backward, and either window can change peak location and threshold crossing. This example illustrates sensitivity only. It is not an onset estimate and should not be generalized from a single trial.

The next step is to confirm the response-direction mapping, document an appropriate preprocessing choice, and examine whether both GMR methods give stable results across reasonable settings. Static or none trials should remain descriptive controls rather than entering onset estimates once that mapping is confirmed.

Source: 02_exploratory_analysis.qmd, “Smoothing sensitivity on a balanced set of example trials.” Data: data/Participant A/Condition_A_Block_1/Trial12.LeftBackgroundSlowTarget.csv. Centered position windows 1, 11, and 21 samples at 1,000 Hz, followed by two centered numerical derivatives. No smoothing settings were chosen from this example.
